title: An asymmetric packing code of radius R is a set of binary n-words so that no binary n-word can be reached from more than
exact_target: Determine the largest binary code whose upward asymmetric radius-R balls are pairwise disjoint.
definition_tex:
\subsection{Definitions and mathematical statement}
For $x\in\{0,1\}^n$ and an integer $R\ge0$, let
\[
 B_R^+(x)=\{y\in\{0,1\}^n:x_i\le y_i\text{ for all }i,
                              \ d_H(x,y)\le R\}.
\]
Thus a channel output is formed by changing at most $R$ zeroes
to ones, without any change in the opposite direction.
An asymmetric packing code is a set $C\subseteq\{0,1\}^n$ whose
upward balls are pairwise disjoint:
\[
             B_R^+(x)\cap B_R^+(x')=\varnothing
                       \qquad(x,x'\in C,\ x\ne x').
\]
Define $A^+(n,R)$ as the largest size of such a code.
Determine this maximum, especially its sharp growth for fixed
$R$ and $n\to\infty$.

Pairwise disjointness means that every possible received word
has at most one codeword that could have produced it with the
allowed errors; it does not require every word to be reachable.
Equivalently, two distinct codewords $x,x'$ cannot both have at
most $R$ ones outside the other's support. Indeed, their
coordinatewise union is the smallest possible common output.
This gives a concrete pairwise feasibility criterion for codes.

The objective is maximization under disjointness. The word
``covering'' in the last sentence of the collected source is a
slip: the preceding definition and this entry concern packing.

\subsection{Short English statement}
Determine the largest binary code whose upward asymmetric radius-R balls are pairwise disjoint.
